name: Price-Momentum
required_data: monthly close prices adjusted for splits and dividends
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Rank stocks each month by past performance over a formation period (usually T=12 months), skipping the most recent S=1 month. Performance can be cumulative return, mean monthly return, or risk-adjusted mean return (mean divided by monthly volatility). Buy the top decile (winners) and short the bottom decile (losers) as a dollar-neutral portfolio, or buy only the top decile for a long-only version. Hold for a set holding period of 1 month or more, using overlapping portfolios for longer holds. Weights are equal (1/N, or ±1/(2N_L) and ±1/(2N_S) for long/short) or proportional to 1/σ or 1/σ².
backtest_note: Results depend on the universe, how deciles are cut, and the weighting scheme, and they need survivorship-bias-free price data.

name: Earnings-Momentum
required_data: quarterly EPS announcements (at least 12 quarters of history); earnings announcement dates; daily close prices
data_sources: FinancialDatasets (earnings, EPS history); IBKR history (daily bars)
gaps: Earnings dates and EPS must be point-in-time (as reported, not restated)
rule_summary: For each stock, compute standardized unexpected earnings: SUE = (latest quarterly EPS minus EPS from 4 quarters earlier) divided by the standard deviation of these unexpected earnings over the last 8 quarters. Build a dollar-neutral portfolio that buys stocks in the top SUE decile and shorts stocks in the bottom SUE decile. Rebalance when new earnings are reported.
backtest_note: The text does not give a holding period or rebalance schedule, so you must pick one (e.g., quarterly) and use point-in-time EPS data to avoid look-ahead bias.

name: Residual Momentum
required_data: monthly stock returns; risk-free rate (1-month T-bill); Fama-French MKT, SMB, HML factor returns
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); Kenneth French data library (factor returns, public)
gaps: Factor returns come in as custom data; point-in-time membership
rule_summary: For each stock, regress monthly excess returns on the Fama-French factors (MKT, SMB, HML) plus an intercept over a 36-month window, skipping the most recent month. Using the estimated betas without the intercept, compute residuals over a 12-month formation period that also skips the most recent month. Rank stocks by the mean residual divided by the residual standard deviation. Buy the top decile and short the bottom decile to form a dollar-neutral portfolio, with equal or non-equal weights. Hold the portfolio for usually 1 month, possibly longer, then rebalance.
backtest_note: Fama-French factor data is publicly available. The main requirement is at least 37 months of return history for each stock.

rule_summary: Pick two historically highly correlated stocks A and B. Compute each stock's return from t1 to t2 (simple or log), then subtract the pair's mean return. Short the stock with a positive demeaned return ("rich") and buy the one with a negative demeaned return ("cheap"). Size the positions as dollar-neutral, with total gross investment I at the prices at entry time t* ≥ t2.
backtest_note: The text does not specify the pair-selection correlation threshold, the lookback t1–t2, or the exit rule, so these must be chosen by the tester.

name: Mean-Reversion—Single Cluster
required_data: daily close prices; industry/sector classification
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Take N > 2 historically highly correlated stocks (e.g., same industry). Compute each stock's log return over a lookback period, subtract the cross-sectional mean return, and set dollar positions D_i = -γ·(demeaned return), so stocks above the mean are shorted and those below are bought. The portfolio is dollar-neutral, and γ = I / Σ|demeaned R_i| scales total gross investment to I.
backtest_note: The text does not specify the return lookback, the rebalance frequency, or how clusters are chosen, so the backtester has to pick these.
name_es: Reversión a la media – grupo único

name: Mean-Reversion—Multiple Clusters
required_data: daily close prices; sector/industry classification
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Group stocks into K clusters of historically highly correlated names, for example sectors. Regress stock returns on a binary cluster-membership matrix with no intercept; the residuals are each stock's return minus its cluster's mean return. Following the base mean-reversion strategy in Section 3.9, short stocks with positive demeaned returns and buy stocks with negative ones. This makes the portfolio dollar-neutral within each cluster. You can also run the strategy separately in each cluster and split capital equally across the K strategies.
backtest_note: You need to choose the return lookback window and how positions are weighted from the base Section 3.9 strategy, plus how clusters are defined (e.g., sectors).
name_es: Reversión a la media – múltiples grupos

name: Mean-Reversion—Weighted Regression
required_data: daily close prices; industry/sector classifications; risk factor loadings; historical volatilities
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Run a weighted cross-sectional regression of stock returns R_i on a loading matrix Ω (industry dummies and/or non-industry risk factors, with intercept), using weights z_i = 1/σ_i² where σ_i is historical volatility. The demeaned returns are R̃_i = z_i ε_i, where ε_i are the regression residuals. These are orthogonal to all factor columns and sum to zero. Following the mean-reversion logic, go long stocks with negative R̃_i and short stocks with positive R̃_i, for example with weights proportional to -R̃_i. Rebalance each period.
backtest_note: The section does not specify the factors in Ω, the return lookback or the rebalance period, so these must be chosen.
name_es: Reversión a la media – regresión ponderada

name: Single Moving Average
required_data: daily close prices
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: For each stock, compute a moving average of past daily prices over T days. This can be a simple MA or an exponential MA with decay factor λ<1. Go long (or close a short) when the current price P is above MA(T), and go short (or close a long) when P is below MA(T). The rule can be run long-only, short-only, or long-short, and applied to each stock separately. With many stocks, the portfolio can be built close to dollar-neutral.
backtest_note: The text gives no values for T or λ, so you have to choose them yourself, along with the position sizing.

name: Two Moving Averages
required_data: daily close prices
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Compute two moving averages of the stock price, a short one MA(T') and a long one MA(T) with T' < T (for example T' = 10 and T = 30 days). Go long (or close shorts) when MA(T') > MA(T), and go short (or close longs) when MA(T') < MA(T). An optional stop-loss closes a long position if the current price P falls below (1 − Δ) times the previous day's price P1, and closes a short position if P rises above (1 + Δ) × P1. The example value is Δ = 2%.
backtest_note: You only need daily prices. You have to choose the type of moving average (SMA or EMA) and the position sizing, because the text does not fix them.

name: Three Moving Averages
required_data: daily close prices
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Compute three moving averages of the price with lengths T1 < T2 < T3 (for example 3, 10, 21). Go long when MA(T1) > MA(T2) > MA(T3), and close the long when MA(T1) ≤ MA(T2). Go short when MA(T1) < MA(T2) < MA(T3), and close the short when MA(T1) ≥ MA(T2).
backtest_note: The rules are fully explicit. The tester still has to choose the MA type (SMA or EMA) and the instrument universe.

name: Support and Resistance
required_data: daily high, low, close prices; intraday prices
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Compute the pivot point C = (previous day's high + low + close)/3, the resistance R = 2C − previous low, and the support S = 2C − previous high. Go long when the current price P > C and close the long when P ≥ R. Go short when P < C and close the short when P ≤ S.
backtest_note: The rules are explicit, but intraday prices are needed to check the current price against C, R and S. The text does not say what to do with open positions at the end of the day.

name: Channel
required_data: daily close prices; trading volume (optional confirmation)
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Compute a Donchian channel for each stock: the ceiling is the maximum and the floor is the minimum of the last T prices. Go long (or close a short) when the price touches the floor, and go short (or close a long) when the price touches the ceiling. If the price breaks through the ceiling or floor, the trader may treat it as a new trend and follow it; a rise in traded volume can be used to confirm the signal.
backtest_note: The text does not give the lookback T, a tolerance for "price equals floor/ceiling", or an exact breakout rule, so these have to be chosen.

name: Event-Driven—M&A
required_data: M&A announcements; deal terms (cash price or exchange ratio); daily close prices; deal completion/failure dates
data_sources: GAP: M&A announcement and deal-terms history; IBKR history (daily bars)
gaps: No deal database; target/acquirer pairs must be built by hand
rule_summary: When a listed company announces it will acquire another listed company at a price different from the target's market price, take positions in the deal. In a cash merger, buy the target's stock. In a stock merger, buy the target (A) and short the acquirer (B) at the exchange ratio (e.g., buy 1 A, short 2 B), then hold until the deal closes or fails.
backtest_note: The backtest needs a survivorship-free M&A deal database with deal terms and outcomes, and the main risk is that a deal fails.

name: Machine Learning—Single-Stock KNN
required_data: daily close prices; daily volume
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: For one stock, predict the cumulative return over the next T trading days with KNN. The features are moving averages of that stock's own price and volume over different lengths, scaled to 0-1 using their min and max over the training period. Find the k nearest past feature vectors by Euclidean distance (or another metric such as Manhattan) and take the average of their realized forward returns, or use a regression-weighted combination of them. Go long if the predicted return is above an upper threshold and go short if it is below a lower threshold.
backtest_note: The text does not give values for T, k, the moving-average lengths, the sample size or the long/short thresholds, so you have to choose them yourself and validate out of sample (for example a 60/40 train/validation split).
name_es: Aprendizaje automático – acción individual con KNN

name: Statistical Arbitrage—Optimization
required_data: daily close prices; expected returns forecasts; covariance matrix (sample or risk model)
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Choose portfolio weights that maximize the expected Sharpe ratio, given expected stock returns E_i and a covariance matrix C. With no constraints and no transaction costs, set weights w_i = γ Σ_j C^-1_ij E_j, scaled so that Σ|w_i| = 1 with γ > 0. To get a dollar-neutral portfolio, maximize the Sharpe ratio subject to a dollar-neutrality constraint.
backtest_note: The text does not say how to compute the expected returns or set the rebalance frequency, and it says a stable model covariance matrix should replace the sample one.

name: Dollar-Neutrality
required_data: daily close prices; expected return signals; covariance matrix (multifactor risk model); risk factor loadings
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Build a dollar-neutral stock portfolio by minimizing the mean-variance objective (λ/2)·w'Cw − E'w − μ·Σw_i. Here E holds the expected returns, which can come from mean-reversion, momentum, machine-learning or other signals, and C is the covariance matrix (usually from a multifactor risk model). The solution is w = (1/λ)·C⁻¹[E − 1·(1'C⁻¹E)/(1'C⁻¹1)], so the weights sum to zero. λ is set so the portfolio meets the total investment level of Eq. 346. Weights rebalance whenever the signals or the covariance matrix are updated.
backtest_note: The section only sets up the optimization: the expected-return signal, the covariance model and the rebalance schedule are left to the user.

name: Market-Making
required_data: intraday quotes (bid/ask); order book / queue position data; tick-level trades; short- and long-horizon alpha signals
data_sources: GAP: historical L1/L2 quotes and trades (tick level)
gaps: Queue position and adverse selection need tick-level book data; IBKR historical ticks are limited
rule_summary: Place passive limit orders to buy at the bid and sell at the ask to capture the spread. To limit adverse selection from informed flow, use a short-horizon signal of price direction: buy at the bid only when the signal predicts a rise, and sell at the ask only when it predicts a fall. Optionally weight this with a longer-horizon (still possibly intraday) signal. When both signals are strong and point the same way, send aggressive orders instead of passive ones.
backtest_note: The text does not define the signals, and realistic fills depend on queue position and latency, so the backtest needs order-book data and a fill model.

name: Alpha Combos
required_data: realized return time series of each alpha; alpha desired holdings/positions; expected returns of alphas (e.g. moving average of returns); daily close prices
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FinancialDatasets (US stock OHLCV)
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias; Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config
rule_summary: Combine a large number N of weak alphas (each gives desired holdings on the same universe, e.g. the 2,500 most liquid US stocks) into one "mega-alpha" and trade it. To get the alpha weights, demean each alpha's realized return series over M+1 periods, compute sample variances, normalize the series, and remove the cross-sectional mean. Then normalize the expected returns E_i by sigma_i and regress them on the remaining factor columns; the weights are proportional to the regression residuals divided by sigma_i.
backtest_note: You must first build or obtain a large set of alphas (for example the 101 formulaic alphas) and choose how to estimate expected returns. The excerpt is cut off before steps 9+, so the final weighting step is inferred from the cited method.

name: Sector Momentum Rotation
required_data: monthly close prices of sector/industry ETFs
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars)
rule_summary: Rank sector/industry ETFs by their cumulative return over a T-month formation period (usually 6 to 12 months). Buy the ETFs in the top decile and hold them for 1 to 3 months, then re-rank. For a dollar-neutral version, also short the ETFs in the bottom decile.
backtest_note: With only a few sector ETFs, decile cuts hold just one or two ETFs each, so you have to choose a breakpoint.

name: Sector Momentum Rotation with MA filter
required_data: daily close prices of sector ETFs
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars)
rule_summary: Rank sector ETFs by momentum over a lookback period T, as in the base sector momentum rotation strategy. Buy ETFs in the top decile only if the current price P is above its moving average MA(T'). Short ETFs in the bottom decile only if P is below MA(T'). MA(T') uses daily prices, and T' can differ from T (for example, 100 to 200 days). Rebalance on the base strategy's schedule.
backtest_note: This section does not give the momentum lookback T or the rebalance frequency, so they must be taken from the base sector rotation strategy. Deciles are coarse when the universe holds only a few sector ETFs.
name_es: Rotación de momentum sectorial con filtro de media móvil

name: Dual-Momentum Sector Rotation
required_data: daily close prices of sector ETFs; daily close prices of market index ETF; daily close prices of uncorrelated ETF (gold or Treasury)
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars)
rule_summary: Rank sector ETFs by cross-sectional momentum, as in the basic sector rotation strategy. If the market index ETF price P is above its moving average MA(T'), buy the top-decile sector ETFs. Otherwise put the money in an ETF that is not correlated with the market, such as a gold ETF or a Treasury ETF. T' is usually 100 to 200 days.
backtest_note: The section does not give the momentum lookback or the rebalance period, so these come from the basic sector rotation strategy (e.g. 12-month momentum with monthly rebalancing).

name: Alpha Rotation
required_data: daily or weekly sector ETF returns; Fama-French 3 factor returns (MKT, SMB, HML)
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); Kenneth French data library (factor returns, public)
rule_summary: For each sector ETF, run a time-series regression of its returns on the Fama-French 3 factors (MKT, SMB, HML) over the estimation period, usually 1 year of daily or weekly returns. Take the intercept as the ETF's alpha. Rank the ETFs by alpha, as in sector momentum rotation: buy the top-decile ETFs and optionally short the bottom-decile ETFs, then rebalance periodically (e.g. monthly).
backtest_note: The decile cutoffs and holding period come from the sector momentum rotation strategy, not from this section, so you need to choose the ETF universe and the rebalance period yourself.

name: R-squared
required_data: ETF returns (daily/weekly/monthly); Fama-French MKT, SMB, HML factors; Carhart MOM factor
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); Kenneth French data library (factor returns, public)
rule_summary: For each ETF, run a time-series regression of its returns on the Fama-French 3 factors plus Carhart momentum, and record the intercept (alpha) and the R². Sort ETFs into quintiles by R², then sort each quintile into sub-quintiles by alpha, giving 25 groups. Go long ETFs with the lowest R² and highest alpha, and short ETFs with the highest R² and lowest alpha. Rebalance at the same frequency and over the same estimation period as alpha rotation (Section 4.2), or use a longer period when returns are monthly.
backtest_note: The section does not fix the estimation window or the rebalance frequency (it defers to alpha rotation), and with few ETFs the 25 groups can each hold very few funds.

name: Mean-reversion
required_data: daily high, low, close prices; historical volatility (optional for weights)
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars)
rule_summary: Compute each ETF's internal bar strength from the previous day: IBS = (Close − Low) / (High − Low), which falls between 0 and 1. Rank the ETF universe cross-sectionally by IBS, short the top decile (expensive) and buy the bottom decile (cheap) in a dollar-neutral portfolio. Weights can be uniform or non-uniform, for example based on historical volatility.
backtest_note: Rules are explicit. The main choices are which ETF universe to use and the daily rebalance timing and costs.

name: Leveraged ETFs (LETFs)
required_data: daily close prices of leveraged and inverse leveraged ETF pairs; Treasury ETF prices; borrow costs / short rebates
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FRED (T-bill rate for short proceeds)
gaps: Borrow fees and availability for leveraged ETFs are not in bar data
rule_summary: Short a leveraged ETF and an inverse leveraged ETF together. Both must have the same leverage (e.g. 2x or 3x) and track the same underlying index. Invest the short-sale proceeds in, for example, a Treasury ETF. The trade profits from the negative long-term drift that daily rebalancing causes in LETFs.
backtest_note: The text gives no rule for the holding period or for rebalancing the short legs, so these must be assumed. Short-borrow costs and availability strongly affect returns, and there is a large short-term risk if one short leg rallies sharply.

name: Multi-asset Trend Following
required_data: daily close prices; historical volatility
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars)
rule_summary: Compute each ETF's cumulative return over a lookback T (e.g. 6-12 months). Keep only ETFs with a positive cumulative return. Optionally, also keep only those whose last close is above their long-term moving average (100-200 days). Go long all remaining ETFs with weights proportional to R, R/σ, or R/σ² (σ = historical volatility), normalized so the weights sum to 1. Optional caps w_i ≤ w_max limit the weight of any one ETF.
backtest_note: The text does not state the rebalance frequency, the volatility window, the ETF universe or the weight cap level, so each must be chosen.
name_es: Seguimiento de la tendencia con múltiples activos

name: Bullets
required_data: bond prices by maturity; yield curve; interest rate forecasts
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: Buy bonds that all mature on the same date T, so the portfolio sits on one point of the yield curve. Pick a long maturity if you expect rates to fall and a short maturity if you expect rates to rise. Buy the bonds gradually over time to reduce interest-rate risk, and hold them.
backtest_note: The choice of maturity depends on the trader's own view of future rates, and the text gives no schedule for spreading the purchases over time.

name: Barbells
required_data: bond prices by maturity; yield curve / interest rates by tenor
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: Buy bonds at only two maturities: a short maturity T1 and a long maturity T2, which combines two bullet portfolios. Choose the weights so the portfolio's modified duration matches a bullet portfolio at a middle maturity T* (T1 < T* < T2). The barbell then has higher convexity than the bullet, which gives better protection against parallel shifts in the yield curve, but at the cost of a lower overall yield.
backtest_note: The text does not specify T1, T2, the weights or a rebalancing rule, so these must be chosen; zero-coupon or Treasury yield curve data is needed.

name: Ladders
required_data: bond prices by maturity; coupon data; yield curve
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: Hold a portfolio of bonds with roughly equal capital in n maturities (e.g. n = 10) that are evenly spaced: T_(i+1) = T_i + δ. When the shortest bonds approach maturity, sell them and buy new bonds at the far end of the ladder, so duration stays about constant. The portfolio maturity is the average of the n maturities. A higher average maturity gives more income but also more interest rate risk.
backtest_note: The text gives no values for the rung spacing δ or the roll timing, and individual bond prices are usually OTC data; a ladder can be approximated with constant-maturity Treasury yields.

name: Bond Immunization
required_data: bond prices and yields; modified durations and convexities; yield curve; liability amount and date
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: To fund a known future cash liability F due at time T*, invest P = F/(1+Yδ)^(T*/δ) in bonds with different maturities. With 2 bonds, pick the dollar amounts P1 and P2 so that P1+P2=P and the portfolio's modified duration equals D = T*/(1+Yδ). With 3 bonds, also match the convexity C = T*(T*+δ)/(1+Yδ)^2. Rebalance the portfolio periodically as the yield curve moves.
backtest_note: You need bond-level price and yield data, which is mostly OTC. The text also assumes one flat yield for all bonds and gives no rebalancing interval.

name: Dollar-Duration-Neutral Butterfly
required_data: bond prices; modified durations; yield curve by tenor
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: Buy a barbell (a short-maturity bond T1 and a long-maturity bond T3) and short a bullet bond with intermediate maturity T2 (T1 < T2 < T3). Choose dollar amounts so the trade costs zero (P1 + P3 = P2) and is dollar-duration neutral (P1·D1 + P3·D3 = P2·D2), with D the modified durations. This hedges parallel yield-curve shifts but leaves exposure to changes in slope and curvature.
backtest_note: The text gives no entry, exit or rebalance rule, and no rule for choosing maturities, so the trader must set these, and getting bond-level price data costs extra.

name: Fifty-Fifty Butterfly
required_data: bond prices; modified durations; yield curve by tenor
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: This is a three-bond butterfly. You take one position in the body (medium maturity) and opposite positions in the short-maturity and long-maturity wings. You size the positions so each wing carries half of the body's dollar duration: P1 D1 = P3 D3 = ½ P2 D2. The trade is dollar-duration neutral and roughly neutral to small steepening or flattening of the curve, but it is not dollar neutral (not zero cost).
backtest_note: The text gives position sizing only. It has no entry, exit or direction signal, so you would have to choose your own signal and rebalancing schedule, and you would need bond-level price and duration data.

name: Regression-Weighted Butterfly
required_data: bond prices; bond durations; historical yields by maturity
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: Build a bond butterfly: go long (or short) the middle-maturity bond (body) and take the opposite position in the short- and long-maturity bonds (wings). Size the positions so the trade is dollar-duration neutral, P1D1 + P3D3 = P2D2, and curve-neutral, P1D1 = β·P3D3. Estimate β by a linear regression of historical changes in the body-minus-short-wing yield spread on changes in the body-minus-long-wing yield spread. Usually β > 1.
backtest_note: The text covers only position sizing. It gives no rule for when to enter or exit, no regression window and no rebalance schedule, so these must be assumed.

name: Maturity-Weighted Butterfly
required_data: bond prices/yields by maturity; bond maturities; bond durations
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public); Treasury futures or bond ETFs as tradable proxies
gaps: No bond instrument type in Nautilus; bond prices must be modelled from the curve or replaced by ETFs/futures
rule_summary: Build a bond butterfly: take a position in the middle-maturity bond (body, T2) and the opposite position in the short (T1) and long (T3) maturity bonds (wings), as in the regression-weighted butterfly. Do not estimate the weighting coefficient β by historical regression. Set it from the maturities instead: β = (T2 − T1)/(T3 − T2). Use β in the wing weights from Eq. (408).
backtest_note: Eq. (408), which gives the position sizing, plus the entry/exit signals and rebalancing schedule are not in this excerpt, so they have to be taken from the parent butterfly section or chosen by the modeller.

name: Low-Risk Factor
required_data: bond credit ratings; bond maturities; bond prices/returns
data_sources: GAP: bond-level prices, ratings and spreads
gaps: Needs a corporate/government bond database
rule_summary: Buy low-risk corporate bonds. In investment grade, keep bonds rated AAA to A- and go long the bottom decile by maturity (the shortest bonds). In high yield, keep bonds rated BB+ to B- and go long the bottom decile by maturity.
backtest_note: Corporate bonds trade OTC, so you need bond-level price and rating data (e.g. index constituents), and the text gives no rebalance frequency, so monthly is an assumption.

name: Value Factor
required_data: bond yields; risk-free rates; credit ratings; bond maturities
data_sources: GAP: bond-level prices, ratings and spreads
gaps: Needs a corporate/government bond database
rule_summary: Run a cross-sectional regression of each bond's credit spread (yield minus risk-free rate) on credit-rating dummies and maturity. The fitted value is the theoretical spread S*. Value is V = ln(S/S*) or S/S* - 1, and the strategy buys the bonds in the top decile by V.
backtest_note: The text gives no rebalance frequency, and corporate bond prices and ratings are OTC or proprietary data.

name: Carry Factor
required_data: bond prices; yield curves by maturity; modified duration; risk-free rate (for funded version)
data_sources: GAP: bond-level prices, ratings and spreads
gaps: Needs a corporate/government bond database
rule_summary: For each bond, compute carry over a period Δt. Assuming a constant term structure, carry = yield × Δt plus roll-down, where roll-down ≈ −modified duration × [R(t, T−Δt) − R(t, T)]. Buy bonds in the top carry decile and short bonds in the bottom decile to build a zero-cost portfolio, then recompute carry and rebalance each period.
backtest_note: The text does not give the carry horizon Δt or the rebalance frequency. You also need yield curves you can interpolate and OTC bond price data.

name: Rolling Down the Yield Curve
required_data: bond prices; yield curve by maturity; bond maturities and coupons
data_sources: FRED / US Treasury par yield curve (public)
gaps: Bond prices modelled from the curve
rule_summary: Buy medium- or long-term bonds in the steepest segments of the yield curve, where the roll-down return is largest. Hold them while they roll down the curve. Sell them before they get close to maturity, and use the proceeds to buy new medium- or long-term bonds in whatever segment of the curve is steepest at that time.
backtest_note: The text does not define the holding period, the sell point near maturity, or how to measure the steepest segment, so these must be modelled; bond price data are OTC.
name_es: Rodando hacia abajo por la curva de rendimientos

name: Yield Curve Spread (Flatteners and Steepeners)
required_data: bond prices/yields by maturity; bond durations; interest rate forecasts
data_sources: IBKR history (Treasury futures ZT/ZF/ZN/ZB); FRED (yields, for the signal)
gaps: Futures DV01 weights need conversion-factor/CTD data; ETF pairs are a simpler proxy
rule_summary: Trade the spread between the yields of two bonds from the same issuer with different maturities. Flattener: if you expect rates to rise, sell the spread, meaning short the shorter-maturity bond (front leg) and buy the longer-maturity bond (back leg). Steepener: if you expect rates to fall, buy the spread, meaning buy the front leg and short the back leg. Match the dollar durations of the two legs so the position is immune to small parallel shifts of the yield curve.
backtest_note: The trade signal comes from an outside forecast of interest rates that the text does not specify, so you have to choose a forecasting model yourself.
name_es: Margen de la curva de rendimientos (Flattener & Steepener)

name: CDS Basis Arbitrage
required_data: bond prices/yields; CDS spreads by tenor; risk-free rates by tenor; bond terms (coupon, maturity)
data_sources: GAP: CDS spreads / swap rates history
gaps: OTC instruments; no source
rule_summary: Compute the CDS basis as the CDS spread minus the bond spread (bond yield minus the risk-free rate). When the basis is negative, the bond is cheap: buy the bond and buy CDS protection on it to lock in a nominally risk-free profit. Hold the position until the basis converges or the bond matures.
backtest_note: Needs OTC CDS quotes and bond prices from dealers. You must also choose how to measure the bond spread (for example the matching risk-free benchmark) and model funding costs.
name_es: Arbitraje de la base del CDS

name: Swap-Spread Arbitrage
instruments: interest rate swaps; government bonds; repo
required_data: swap rates by tenor; Treasury yields by maturity; LIBOR rates; repo rates
data_sources: GAP: CDS spreads / swap rates history
gaps: OTC instruments; no source
rule_summary: Go long (short) a fixed-for-floating interest rate swap, receiving (paying) the fixed swap rate against LIBOR. At the same time, short (buy) a Treasury bond with the same maturity, financed at the repo rate, so the position is dollar-neutral. P&L accrues at ±[(swap rate − Treasury yield) − (LIBOR − repo rate)]. The long-swap version pays off if LIBOR falls, so the trade is a bet on LIBOR.
backtest_note: The text gives no rule for choosing the long or short side and no rule for entering or exiting the trade, and you need OTC swap rates and repo rate data to test it.

name: Cash-and-carry Arbitrage
required_data: intraday index futures prices; intraday prices of index constituents; index weights; expected dividends of constituents; risk-free rate; transaction cost estimates
data_sources: IBKR history (index futures and ETF/basket bars); FRED (rates); GAP: dividend forecasts
gaps: Fair basis needs dividends and financing rates
rule_summary: Compute the fair futures price F* = (S − D)·exp(r(T−t)), where D is the discounted value of dividends paid before delivery. The basis is B = (F − F*)/S. If |B| is larger than transaction costs, sell the futures and buy the index basket when B > 0, or buy the futures and short the basket when B < 0. Close the position when the basis returns to zero.
backtest_note: These opportunities last only a short time and need synchronized high-frequency data, dividend forecasts and realistic slippage/execution modelling, so results depend heavily on those assumptions.

name: Dispersion Trading in Equity Indexes
required_data: option chains with implied volatility for index and constituents; index weights and shares outstanding; daily close prices for historical correlations; index level
data_sources: GAP: historical option chains for index and constituents
gaps: Needs option quotes for the index and its members
rule_summary: Buy near-ATM straddles on each index constituent and sell one near-ATM straddle on the index. Hold n_i = S_i*P_I / sum_j(S_j*P_j) straddles on stock i, where S_i is shares outstanding and the index is cap-weighted. The trade is put on when index implied volatility is well above the theoretical index volatility, which is computed from the constituent implied volatilities and the historical correlation matrix. All options have about 1 month to expiry, and the positions are held until expiry.
backtest_note: The text gives no numeric entry threshold or correlation lookback, and you need full option data for every constituent, which is expensive to get.
name_es: Trading de dispersión en índices de acciones

name: Dispersion Trading: Subset Portfolio
required_data: option chains with implied volatility; daily close prices; index weights
data_sources: GAP: historical option chains for index and constituents
gaps: Needs option quotes for the index and its members
rule_summary: Sell ATM straddles on the index (e.g. S&P 500) when its implied volatility is above the theoretical index volatility, and buy ATM straddles on only a subset of the constituent stocks. Theoretical index volatility uses a statistical risk model correlation matrix: keep the top K principal components of the sample correlation matrix (e.g. daily close-to-close returns over 1 year, about 252 days), with K set by eRank, and add a specific-risk diagonal. The long leg holds straddles on the N* stocks with the lowest specific-risk contribution w_i^2 σ_i^2 ξ_i^2 (e.g. N* = 100 for the S&P 500).
backtest_note: The text does not give straddle sizing, maturity or exit rules, and you need historical option implied-volatility data for every constituent stock.
name_es: Trading de dispersión – subconjunto del portafolio

name: Intraday Arbitrage Between Index ETFs
required_data: intraday quotes (bid/ask)
data_sources: GAP: synchronized intraday bid/ask quotes for SPY/IVV/VOO
gaps: IBKR historical bid/ask ticks are limited in depth and speed
rule_summary: Trade two ETFs that track the same index, for example SPY and IVV. If ETF1's bid is at least ETF2's ask × κ, buy ETF2 and sell ETF1. Close that position once ETF2's bid is at least ETF1's ask. Do the reverse the same way: if ETF2's bid is at least ETF1's ask × κ, buy ETF1 and sell ETF2, and close once ETF1's bid is at least ETF2's ask. κ is a threshold close to 1, for example 1.002. Execute with fill-or-kill limit orders.
backtest_note: The backtest needs tick-level synchronized bid/ask quotes and a realistic model of fill-or-kill fills and latency, because these arbitrage opportunities last only a very short time.
name_es: Arbitraje intradía entre ETFs de índices

name: Index Volatility Targeting with Risk-Free Asset
instruments: ETFs; equity index futures; cash / money market; government bonds
required_data: daily index prices; implied volatility index (e.g. VIX) or volatility forecast; risk-free rate / T-bill returns
data_sources: IBKR history (daily bars); FRED (T-bill rate)
rule_summary: Split capital between a stock index and a risk-free asset such as Treasury bills. Put weight w = σ*/σ in the index, where σ* is the target volatility and σ is the index volatility (usually implied, or a volatility forecast), and put 1−w in the risk-free asset. If there is a maximum leverage L, w cannot exceed L. Rebalance on a fixed schedule (weekly, monthly, etc.), or only when the percentage change |Δw|/w since the last rebalance is larger than a threshold κ.
backtest_note: You have to pick the target σ*, the leverage cap L, the threshold κ and the volatility estimate yourself, because the text gives no values.
name_es: Targeting de volatilidad sobre índice con activo libre de

name: VIX Futures Basis Trading
required_data: daily VIX index level; daily front-month VIX futures prices; VIX futures settlement dates; front-month mini-S&P 500 futures prices
data_sources: Cboe CFE VX futures settlement history (public); Cboe VIX index history (public)
gaps: VX trades on CFE, not CME, so roboquant.dev has no data for it
rule_summary: Compute the daily roll D = (UX1 − VIX)/T, where UX1 is the front-month VIX futures price and T is the number of business days to settlement (at least 10). Open a long UX1 position when D < −0.10 (backwardation) and close it when D > −0.05. Open a short UX1 position when D > 0.10 (contango) and close it when D < 0.05. You can hedge volatility spikes with front-month mini-S&P 500 futures, using a hedge ratio from a historical regression of VIX futures price changes on mini-S&P returns.
backtest_note: The rules are explicit. You need to decide how to roll contracts when fewer than 10 days remain to settlement, and how to estimate the hedge ratio.
name_es: Trading de la base de futuros del VIX

name: Volatility Carry with Two ETNs
required_data: daily close prices of VXX and VXZ
data_sources: IBKR history (VXX, VXZ or successors); Cboe CFE VX futures history (public)
gaps: Original VXX/VXZ ETNs matured in 2019; use relaunched VXX and a mid-term substitute
rule_summary: Short VXX, which holds short-term VIX futures (months 1-2), and buy VXZ, which holds medium-term VIX futures (months 4-7). This captures the larger roll (contango) loss in VXX. A serial regression of returns sets the hedge ratio between the two ETNs.
backtest_note: The text does not specify the regression window or the rebalance frequency, and short-term VXX spikes can cause large drawdowns.
name_es: Carry de volatilidad con dos ETNs

name: Hedging Short VXX with VIX Futures
required_data: daily VXX prices; VIX futures prices by maturity; historical covariance/correlation of returns
data_sources: IBKR history (VXX, VXZ or successors); Cboe CFE VX futures history (public)
gaps: Original VXX/VXZ ETNs matured in 2019; use relaunched VXX and a mid-term substitute
rule_summary: Short VXX and hedge it with a long basket of N mid-maturity VIX futures (for example, 4–7 month maturities, like the VXZ). The basket weights come from a serial regression with intercept of VXX returns on the futures returns, which minimizes tracking error: w_i = σ_X Σ_j C^-1_ij σ_j ρ_j. You can add the constraints w_i ≥ 0 and Σw_i = 1 (dollar-neutral), or minimize total portfolio variance instead. Rebalance monthly or more often.
backtest_note: The main modelling choices are which futures maturities to use, the estimation window and the weight constraints. Building rolling futures return series also needs care.
name_es: Cobertura del VXX con futuros del VIX

name: Volatility Risk Premium
required_data: VIX index levels; S&P 500 daily close prices; S&P 500 option chains (bid/ask)
data_sources: GAP: historical SPX/SPY option chains; Cboe VIX index history (public)
gaps: Needs option quotes
rule_summary: Sell straddles on S&P 500 options to collect the volatility risk premium. As a proxy for the premium, take the VIX at the start of the current month minus the realized volatility (in %) of daily S&P 500 returns since the start of that month. If this spread is positive, sell straddles.
backtest_note: The text does not give the straddle maturity, strike choice, holding period or how realized vol is measured early in the month, so these must be chosen, and historical SPX option data is needed.

name: Volatility Risk Premium with Gamma Hedging
instruments: index options; equity index futures; ETFs
required_data: option chains with implied volatility; intraday or daily underlying index prices; option Greeks (Delta, Gamma)
data_sources: GAP: historical SPX/SPY option chains; Cboe VIX index history (public)
gaps: Needs option quotes
rule_summary: Sell ATM straddles (short ATM call and put) on the S&P 500 index to collect the volatility risk premium, as in the base strategy. Keep the position close to Delta-neutral with Gamma hedging: buy the underlying when it moves up and sell it when it moves down. The trade then earns Theta decay on the short options, minus the cost of hedging.
backtest_note: The text gives no maturity, re-hedge frequency or Delta threshold, so the hedging schedule and transaction costs have to be modelled.
name_es: Prima de riesgo de volatilidad con cobertura de

name: Volatility Skew—Long Risk Reversal
required_data: option chains with implied volatility; option bid/ask prices; underlying prices
data_sources: GAP: historical SPX/SPY option chains; Cboe VIX index history (public)
gaps: Needs option quotes
rule_summary: Buy OTM call options and sell OTM put options on the same underlying (a long risk reversal). The trade collects the volatility skew, since OTM puts usually carry higher implied volatility than OTM calls at the same distance from the strike. The position is directional: it loses money if the underlying falls below the put strike minus the net premium received.
backtest_note: The text gives no strike distance, maturity, holding period or roll rule, so a backtest has to pick these itself and needs historical option data.

name: Volatility Trading with Variance Swaps
required_data: daily close prices of underlying; variance swap strikes (implied variance); implied volatility
data_sources: GAP: variance swap quotes (OTC) or option strips for replication
gaps: OTC instrument
rule_summary: Go long a variance swap when you expect future realized volatility to be higher than current implied volatility. Go short when you expect it to be lower. At maturity T the swap pays N × (v(T) − K), where v(T) is the annualized realized variance from daily log returns (F = 252, mean not subtracted) and K is the preset variance strike. This removes the need to delta-hedge. One example is dispersion: sell a variance swap on an index and buy variance swaps on its constituents.
backtest_note: Variance swaps trade OTC, so you need historical strike quotes or a model (e.g., to replicate them from option chains). The text gives no explicit signal for when to go long or short.
name_es: Trading de volatilidad con swaps de varianza

name: Moving Averages with HP Filter
required_data: monthly FX spot rates
data_sources: IBKR history (IDEALPRO FX bars or CME FX futures)
rule_summary: Apply the Hodrick-Prescott filter to the FX spot rate series (usually monthly data over several years) to remove high-frequency noise and keep the low-frequency trend S*(t). A typical smoothing parameter is λ = 100×n², with n = 12 for monthly data. Compute a short moving average MA(T1) and a long moving average MA(T2), T1 < T2, on S*(t). Buy the currency pair when MA(T1) > MA(T2) and sell when MA(T1) < MA(T2).
backtest_note: The text does not give T1 or T2. The two-sided HP filter uses future data, so a backtest must re-estimate it at each step using only past data (one-sided) to avoid look-ahead bias.

name: Carry Trade
required_data: FX spot rates; FX forward rates; short-term risk-free interest rates by currency
data_sources: IBKR history (FX spot bars); FRED / central-bank short rates (public)
gaps: Nautilus has no FX forward type; model carry as a daily rate-differential accrual or use CME FX futures
rule_summary: Sell FX forwards on currencies at a forward premium (forward rate F(t,T) above spot S(t), i.e. low-interest-rate currencies). Buy forwards on currencies at a forward discount (F(t,T) below spot, i.e. high-interest-rate currencies). This is the same as borrowing low-rate currencies and lending high-rate currencies without hedging the FX risk. Positions are held to the forward maturity T and then rolled.
backtest_note: The text does not give the forward tenor, how many currencies to trade or how to weight them. Forward prices are OTC, but they can be built from spot rates and interest rates using covered interest parity.

name: High-minus-low Carry
required_data: FX spot rates; 1-month FX forward rates; short-term interest rates by currency (alternative to forwards)
data_sources: IBKR history (FX spot bars); FRED / central-bank short rates (public)
gaps: Nautilus has no FX forward type; model carry as a daily rate-differential accrual or use CME FX futures
rule_summary: For each foreign currency, compute the forward discount D = ln(spot) − ln(forward), which is roughly the foreign minus the domestic interest rate. Buy forwards on currencies in the top quantile by forward discount and sell forwards on currencies in the matching bottom quantile, making a zero-cost, dollar-neutral portfolio. The example uses one-month forwards, so the portfolio is rolled and rebalanced monthly.
backtest_note: FX forwards trade over the counter, so the backtest needs forward quotes or forward rates built from interest-rate differentials, and the quantile cutoff must be chosen.

name: Dollar Carry Trade
required_data: FX spot rates; FX forward rates by tenor (1-12 months)
data_sources: IBKR history (FX spot bars); FRED / central-bank short rates (public)
gaps: Nautilus has no FX forward type; model carry as a daily rate-differential accrual or use CME FX futures
rule_summary: Compute the average forward discount D(t,T) across a basket of N foreign currencies, where each forward discount compares the forward rate with the spot rate. If the average is positive, go long the forwards of all N foreign currencies with equal weights. If it is negative, go short all of them with equal weights. The forward maturity T can be 1, 2, 3, 6 or 12 months, and the position is reset at each maturity.
backtest_note: FX forwards trade over the counter, so you need forward quotes or must build them from interest-rate differentials, and you have to pick the currency basket.

name: Momentum and Carry Combo
required_data: daily FX spot rates; FX forward rates or interest rate differentials; historical returns of momentum and carry strategies
data_sources: IBKR history (FX spot bars); FRED / central-bank short rates (public)
gaps: Nautilus has no FX forward type; model carry as a daily rate-differential accrual or use CME FX futures
rule_summary: Run the FX momentum strategy (Section 8.1) and the FX carry strategy (Section 8.2) together and combine them. One simple way is an equal-weight combo. Another sets the weights w1 and w2 (summing to 1) to minimize the historical variance of the combined return, using sample variances and correlation of the two strategies' returns: w1 = (σ2² − σ1σ2ρ)/(σ1² + σ2² − 2σ1σ2ρ), w2 = (σ1² − σ1σ2ρ)/(σ1² + σ2² − 2σ1σ2ρ).
backtest_note: FX forward prices are OTC data, and the user has to choose the estimation window and rebalance schedule for the weights.

name: FX Triangular Arbitrage
required_data: intraday quotes (bid/ask); synchronized tick data for three currency pairs
data_sources: GAP: synchronized tick-level FX quotes
gaps: Profit depends on latency; bar data cannot test it
rule_summary: Use three currencies A, B, C and compute the round-trip rate R(A→B→C→A) = Bid(A→B) × Bid(B→C) / Ask(C→A). If R > 1, exchange A for B, B for C, and C back to A to lock in a profit. Check the reverse chain (A→C→B→A) the same way.
backtest_note: These opportunities last only moments, so a backtest needs synchronized, executable tick-level bid/ask quotes and a realistic model of latency and fills.

name: Roll Yields
required_data: front-month and second-month futures prices; contract expiry dates; daily futures prices for roll returns
data_sources: IBKR history (expired futures, about 2 years back); Databento CME (via roboquant.dev or direct; rights decision)
gaps: Long history of individual expiries needs Databento or another CME source
rule_summary: For each commodity, compute phi = P1/P2, where P1 is the front-month futures price and P2 is the second-month futures price. phi > 1 means backwardation and phi < 1 means contango. Build a zero-cost long-short portfolio: go long the futures with higher phi and short the futures with lower phi. Roll the contracts into later maturities as they near expiry.
backtest_note: The text does not specify the quantile cutoffs, the weighting, or the rebalance and roll timing, so you have to choose these yourself.

name: Trading Based on Hedging Pressure
required_data: CFTC COT weekly positions (hedgers/commercial and speculators/non-commercial, long and short); commodity futures prices (continuous front-month series)
data_sources: CFTC Commitments of Traders (public); IBKR history (futures bars)
gaps: COT is weekly with a 3-day release lag; use release dates
rule_summary: For each commodity, compute hedging pressure (HP) separately for hedgers and speculators from the weekly CFTC COT report: long contracts divided by total long plus short contracts. Split the universe into top and bottom halves by speculators' HP. Buy futures in the top half that are also in the bottom quintile of hedgers' HP, and sell futures in the bottom half that are also in the top quintile of hedgers' HP. The result is a zero-cost portfolio, with formation and holding periods typically 6 months each.
backtest_note: COT data is public, but you still have to choose how to average HP over the 6-month formation window, how to roll the futures, and how to deal with a small universe where the double sort leaves few names.
name_es: Trading basado en la presión de cobertura

name: Portfolio Diversification with Commodities
required_data: daily close prices; commodity futures prices or index; Fed discount rate history
data_sources: IBKR history (futures or commodity ETF bars)
gaps: Continuous futures need a roll rule
rule_summary: Add commodities to a stock portfolio because commodities have low correlation with equities. Passive approach: put a fixed share of capital into commodities, hold, and rebalance back to the target weights on a set schedule (for example, monthly or yearly). Active approach: raise commodity exposure when the Fed discount rate goes up and cut it when the rate goes down, or use some other timing method.
backtest_note: The text gives no allocation percentages and no exact size of the tilt for the active rule, so these must be picked by the tester.

name: Value
required_data: monthly commodity spot prices (5+ years history); commodity futures prices for implementation
data_sources: IBKR history (futures or commodity ETF bars)
gaps: Continuous futures need a roll rule
rule_summary: For each commodity, compute value as v = P5/P0, where P5 is the spot price 5 years ago and P0 is the current spot price. Build a zero-cost portfolio that buys commodities in the top value tercile and sells those in the bottom tercile. Rebalance monthly.
backtest_note: Spot prices are often proxied by front-month futures, often averaged around the 5-year-ago date, and positions are taken in futures that must be rolled.

name: Skewness Premium
required_data: daily futures prices / returns; continuous futures roll series
data_sources: IBKR history (futures or commodity ETF bars)
gaps: Continuous futures need a roll rule
rule_summary: For each commodity future, compute the skewness of its historical returns over T observations. Go long the futures in the bottom skewness quintile and short those in the top quintile, which gives a zero-cost portfolio. The section does not give the lookback length or the rebalancing frequency.
backtest_note: You must choose the skewness lookback window, the rebalance frequency (monthly is assumed here) and the roll method, because the text does not specify them.

name: Trading with Pricing Models
required_data: futures prices across maturities (term structure); spot prices; historical data for parameter calibration
data_sources: IBKR history (futures bars); GAP: inventory/storage data for the pricing model
gaps: Pricing-model inputs are not specified
rule_summary: Model the log spot price of a commodity as a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Fit its parameters (mean-reversion speed κ, long-run mean a, volatility σ) to historical futures term-structure data, for example with nonlinear least squares, and compute the model futures price for each maturity. Buy futures whose market price is below the model price (cheap) and sell futures whose market price is above it (rich). Check that the model also predicts well out of sample.
backtest_note: The text does not specify the calibration window, how big a mispricing must be to trade, position sizing, or how often to rebalance, so these modelling choices must be made by the user.

name: Hedging Risk with Futures
required_data: futures prices by delivery date; spot commodity prices; planned physical purchase/sale quantities and dates
data_sources: IBKR history (futures and the hedged asset)
gaps: This is a hedge overlay; test it as variance reduction, not as a stand-alone return stream
rule_summary: A trader who expects to buy (sell) a quantity X of a commodity at a future time T buys (sells) at time t a futures contract with delivery date T for that quantity. This locks in the price and hedges the risk of a price rise (fall) between t and T. The position is held until T.
backtest_note: The hedge depends on an assumed physical exposure (quantity and date), so it can only be tested as hedge effectiveness against that assumed exposure, not as a standalone strategy.

name: Cross-Hedging
required_data: spot prices of hedged asset; futures prices on related asset; historical price series for hedge ratio regression
data_sources: IBKR history (futures and the hedged asset)
gaps: This is a hedge overlay; test it as variance reduction, not as a stand-alone return stream
rule_summary: To hedge an asset that has no futures contract of its own, the trader holds the asset and shorts a futures contract on a different asset with similar characteristics, keeping the position until maturity T. The base case uses a hedge ratio of 1. In practice the optimal hedge ratio is estimated, for example with a time-series regression of spot price changes on futures price changes.
backtest_note: This is a hedge, not a return-seeking rule: the hedged asset, the proxy future and the hedge-ratio method all have to be chosen by the user.

name: Interest Rate Risk Hedging
required_data: bond prices; interest rate futures prices; conversion factors; bond and futures dollar durations; yield changes for beta estimation
data_sources: IBKR history (futures and the hedged asset)
gaps: This is a hedge overlay; test it as variance reduction, not as a stand-alone return stream
rule_summary: Hedge interest rate risk on a fixed-income position with interest rate futures. Buy futures (long hedge) to protect against falling rates, or sell futures (short hedge) to protect against rising rates. Set the hedge ratio with the conversion factor model (h = C × MB/MF, used for deliverable bonds) or with the modified-duration model (h = β × DB/DF, where DB and DF are dollar durations and β is often 1). The hedge P&L is the change in the futures basis.
backtest_note: This is a hedging overlay, not a standalone alpha rule, and the text gives no rebalancing schedule or β estimation method.
name_es: Cobertura de riesgo de tasa de interés

name: Calendar Spread
required_data: futures prices by maturity; supply/demand fundamental forecasts
data_sources: IBKR history (expired futures, about 2 years back); Databento CME (rights decision)
gaps: Individual expiries over long history
rule_summary: A bull spread buys the nearby futures contract and sells a deferred-month contract on the same underlying. A bear spread does the reverse. The trader opens a bull spread when they expect low supply and high demand, and a bear spread when they expect high supply and low demand. The idea is that nearby commodity contracts react more strongly than deferred contracts to changes in supply and demand.
backtest_note: The signal is a discretionary view on supply and demand, so a backtest needs a fundamental forecast model that the text does not specify.

name: Contrarian Trading (Mean-Reversion)
required_data: daily futures prices (continuous series); historical volatilities
data_sources: IBKR history (futures bars)
gaps: Continuous futures need a roll rule
rule_summary: Compute each future's return over the last week and the equal-weighted market return Rm across N futures. Set weights wi = -γ(Ri - Rm), with γ chosen so the absolute weights sum to 1. This buys the losers and sells the winners relative to the index, and the portfolio is dollar-neutral. Weights may be scaled by 1/σi or 1/σi² (historical volatility) to avoid over-investing in volatile futures. Rebalance weekly.
backtest_note: You need continuous futures series with rollover rules, and you must choose the futures universe and the volatility lookback window.

name: Contrarian Trading—Market Activity
required_data: daily futures prices; daily futures volume; daily open interest
data_sources: IBKR history (futures bars and volume); GAP: daily open interest per contract (Databento statistics or exchange data)
gaps: Open interest history
rule_summary: Each week, compute the volume factor v = ln(V/V0) for each future, where V is the sum of daily volume over the last week and V0 is the sum over the week before. Compute the open-interest factor u = ln(U/U0) the same way. Keep the futures in the top half by v, then within that set keep the bottom half by u. Apply the basic contrarian rule to this subset: weights equal minus the scaled deviation of each future's last-week return from the cross-sectional mean. This means buying recent losers and shorting recent winners, rebalanced weekly.
backtest_note: The modeller must choose a contract roll method and how to build continuous volume and open-interest series across contracts.

name: Trend Following (Momentum)
required_data: daily futures prices (continuous series); historical volatilities
data_sources: IBKR history (futures bars)
gaps: Continuous futures need a roll rule
rule_summary: For each futures contract, compute the cumulative return R_i over a lookback period T (days, weeks or months) and set the signal eta_i = sign(R_i). Set weights w_i = gamma * eta_i / sigma_i, where sigma_i is historical volatility and gamma makes the absolute weights sum to 1. Optional variants: smooth the signal with eta_i = tanh(R_i/kappa); make the book dollar-neutral by demeaning the weights, or by using separate scale factors gamma+ and gamma- for longs and shorts; or use returns net of the market-index return so that winners are bought and losers are sold relative to the index.
backtest_note: The text leaves the lookback period, rebalance frequency and futures roll method open, so the user has to choose them.

name: Carry, Equity Tranche—Index Hedging
required_data: tranche spreads/upfronts; CDS index spreads; tranche and index durations (or sensitivities); default and recovery data
data_sources: GAP: CDX/iTraxx tranche and index quotes, MBS prices
gaps: OTC structured credit; no data source and no instrument type
rule_summary: Buy (sell protection on) the equity tranche, the lowest-quality tranche of a CDO, and delta-hedge it by selling (buying protection on) the underlying CDS index. The hedge ratio is Delta = D / D_ix, the tranche duration divided by the index duration. The strategy earns carry because the equity tranche premiums are larger than the index premiums. The main risk is credit events hitting the equity tranche.
backtest_note: Needs OTC tranche and index pricing plus a model to compute durations, and the text gives no rebalance rule.
name_es: Carry, tramo de capital – cobertura con índice

name: Carry, Senior/Mezzanine—Index Hedging
required_data: CDO tranche spreads/prices; CDS index spreads; default correlation / pricing model inputs for tranche Delta
data_sources: GAP: CDX/iTraxx tranche and index quotes, MBS prices
gaps: OTC structured credit; no data source and no instrument type
rule_summary: Sell protection on a high-quality CDO tranche (senior or mezzanine). Hedge to Delta-neutrality by buying protection on the underlying CDS index. The hedge ratio is the tranche Delta, i.e. the sensitivity of the tranche value to the index spread.
backtest_note: You need OTC tranche and index price data plus a pricing model, such as Gaussian copula, to compute the Delta. No rebalance frequency is given; daily is an assumption.

name: Carry—Tranche Hedging
required_data: tranche spreads/quotes; tranche risky durations; CDS index data
data_sources: GAP: CDX/iTraxx tranche and index quotes, MBS prices
gaps: OTC structured credit; no data source and no instrument type
rule_summary: Buy a low-quality (junior) CDO tranche and hedge its delta by selling a high-quality (senior) tranche. The hedge ratio is the risky duration of the low tranche divided by the risky duration of the high tranche (Δ_high = D_low / D_high). The position earns the carry (spread difference) between the two tranches.
backtest_note: The trade needs OTC tranche prices, and the risky durations have to come from a model; the text gives no rebalancing rule.

name: Carry—CDS Hedging
required_data: CDO tranche spreads/premiums; single-name CDS spreads; risky durations of tranche and CDS; default/recovery assumptions for pricing
data_sources: GAP: CDX/iTraxx tranche and index quotes, MBS prices
gaps: OTC structured credit; no data source and no instrument type
rule_summary: Buy (sell protection on) a low-quality CDO tranche to collect its high premiums. Hedge the position's delta by buying protection on a single-name CDS whose premiums are lower than the tranche's, rather than hedging with the index or a higher-quality tranche. The hedge ratio is the tranche's risky duration D divided by the CDS risky duration D_CDS (Eq. 489).
backtest_note: You need OTC tranche and CDS prices plus a model for risky durations, and the text gives no rebalancing schedule.

name: CDOs—Curve Trades
required_data: CDO tranche spreads by maturity; tranche notionals; risky durations; tranche MTM valuations
data_sources: GAP: CDX/iTraxx tranche and index quotes, MBS prices
gaps: OTC structured credit; no data source and no instrument type
rule_summary: To trade a flattener, buy short-maturity protection on a CDO tranche and sell long-maturity protection on the same tranche. This pays off if the spread between long and short maturities narrows. A steepener is the reverse trade. The two legs can be sized to be notional-neutral, risky-duration-neutral or carry-neutral, and P&L is the difference between the mark-to-market values of the long and short legs.
backtest_note: CDO tranche prices are OTC, so they are hard to get, and the text gives no entry or exit signal. You must choose the timing rule and the neutrality weighting yourself.

name: Mortgage-Backed Security (MBS) Trading
required_data: passthrough MBS prices; 5-year swap rates; swap curve by tenor; prepayment data (if model-based)
data_sources: GAP: CDX/iTraxx tranche and index quotes, MBS prices
gaps: OTC structured credit; no data source and no instrument type
rule_summary: Buy a passthrough MBS and hedge its interest-rate exposure with interest rate swaps. The hedge ratio is the first derivative of the MBS price P with respect to the 5-year swap rate R. You can get it from a prepayment model, or estimate it non-parametrically from historical data with a constrained regression where P is a non-increasing function of R. The text gives no rebalance rule, so you update the hedge as the estimated derivative changes.
backtest_note: You need OTC MBS and swap prices, and the hedge ratio depends on the choice of prepayment model or regression setup; the text gives no rebalance frequency.

name: Convertible Arbitrage
required_data: convertible bond prices and terms (conversion ratio, issue date); daily stock prices; stock volatility and interest rates for a convertible pricing model; credit spreads
data_sources: GAP: convertible bond prices and terms; IBKR history (underlying stock)
gaps: Convertibles are not in our data or Nautilus instrument set
rule_summary: Buy a newly issued convertible bond, which tends to be underpriced at issuance. At the same time, short h = Δ × C shares of the underlying stock, where C is the conversion ratio and Δ = ∂V/∂S is the model-dependent delta of the conversion option. Rebalance the hedge ratio daily and hold the position for 6 to 12 months from the issue date.
backtest_note: Convertible bond prices trade OTC and are hard to obtain, and the delta depends on which pricing model you choose.

name: Convertible Option-Adjusted Spread
required_data: convertible bond market prices; bond cash flows and terms; Treasury zero-coupon curve; underlying stock prices and volatility for option pricing
data_sources: GAP: convertible bond prices and terms; IBKR history (underlying stock)
gaps: Convertibles are not in our data or Nautilus instrument set
rule_summary: Take two convertible bonds from the same issuer. Buy the one with the higher option-adjusted spread (OAS) and short the one with the lower OAS, and profit if the two spreads converge. To get the OAS, price the convertible as P_C = P_B + V, where P_B is the straight bond value and V is the call option value. Then shift the Treasury zero-coupon curve in parallel (for example with bisection) until V = P_C(market) − P_B. That parallel shift is the OAS.
backtest_note: You need OTC convertible bond prices and a model-dependent OAS calculation, and the text gives no rule for when to exit.
name_es: Diferencial ajustado por opciones de convertible

name: Municipal Bond Tax Arbitrage
required_data: municipal bond yields/prices; borrowing interest rates; corporate tax rate
gaps: Profit depends on the tax status of the investor; not a market backtest
rule_summary: Borrow money and buy tax-exempt municipal bonds. The interest expense is deducted from taxable income (tax shield), so the return is R = r_long − r_short(1 − τ), where r_long is the muni bond yield, r_short is the borrowing rate and τ is the corporate tax rate. Hold the position as long as the after-tax carry stays positive.
backtest_note: The return comes from tax treatment, so a backtest has to assume a tax rate, a financing rate and that interest is deductible, and muni bond prices are OTC and illiquid.

name: Cross-Border Tax Arbitrage
required_data: dividend announcements and ex-dividend dates; daily close prices; tax credit rates by jurisdiction; securities lending / swap terms
gaps: Profit depends on the tax status of the investor; not a market backtest
rule_summary: This applies to stocks in countries with dividend imputation systems, such as Australia, where domestic investors get dividend tax credits but foreign investors do not. The foreign investor sells the stock cum-dividend and buys it back ex-dividend, because the price drop is expected to be larger than the dividend, about D(1+κ) where κ is the tax credit rate. Instead of selling, the investor can lend the stock to a domestic investor cum-dividend and get it back ex-dividend with a pre-agreed share of the tax credit, or use an equivalent swap.
backtest_note: You can test the sell/buy-back version on ex-dividend price drops, but the lending and swap versions need private deal terms and tax-law details for each jurisdiction.

name: Cross-Border Tax Arbitrage with Options
required_data: stock prices; American put option prices; dividend declarations and ex-dividend dates; tax credit rates by country
gaps: Profit depends on the tax status of the investor; not a market backtest
rule_summary: A foreign trader who cannot use the dividend tax credit sells the stock cum-dividend at price S0. At the same time the trader sells a deep in-the-money American put, whose price should already include the tax credit: V_put ≈ K − [S0 − D(1+κ)]. A local holder who can use the credit exercises the put ex-dividend at strike K, so the trader buys the shares back at K. The P&L is S0 + V_put − K = D(1+κ).
backtest_note: A backtest needs option chains around ex-dividend dates, tax credit rates for each country, and a model of when the put holder exercises early. Whether put prices actually include the tax credit is an assumption that must be checked in the data.

name: Inflation Hedging—Inflation Swaps
required_data: inflation swap rates by tenor; CPI index values; Treasury and TIPS yields by maturity
data_sources: GAP: inflation swap rates; FRED (breakeven inflation, CPI)
gaps: OTC; TIP versus IEF ETFs is only a rough proxy
rule_summary: Buy an inflation swap to go long inflation: pay a fixed rate K (the breakeven, usually the Treasury minus TIPS yield spread at the same maturity) and receive a floating rate based on CPI. Sell the swap to take the opposite position. In a zero-coupon swap there is one net payment at maturity T of (I(T)/I(0) − 1) − ((1+K)^T − 1). In a year-on-year swap the parties exchange I(t)/I(t−1) − 1 against K each year.
backtest_note: Inflation swaps trade OTC, so historical swap quotes are hard to get, and the text gives no rule for when to enter or exit; it only describes the hedge structure.
name_es: Cobertura contra la inflación – swaps de inflación

name: TIPS-Treasury Arbitrage
required_data: Treasury bond prices and coupons; TIPS prices and coupons; zero-coupon inflation swap rates by maturity; STRIPS prices (discount factors); CPI index values
data_sources: GAP: TIPS and nominal bond prices, inflation swaps
gaps: Bond-level data
rule_summary: Short a nominal Treasury bond. Hedge it with a synthetic copy: buy a TIPS with the same maturity, and sell zero-coupon inflation swaps (paying fixed rate K) at each coupon date, with notionals equal to the coupon plus principal at maturity. This turns the CPI-linked payments into fixed ones. Use small long or short STRIPS positions to cover the gap between the Treasury coupons/principal and the synthetic payments. Enter when the net upfront cash flow C(0) = P_Treasury − P_TIPS − sum of STRIPS costs is positive, and hold to maturity, since all later cash flows offset each other.
backtest_note: Needs OTC inflation swap quotes and matched TIPS/Treasury/STRIPS prices. Funding and shorting costs also need to be modelled.

name: Weather Risk—Demand Hedging
required_data: daily min/max temperatures; weather-sensitive demand series; HDD/CDD futures and option prices
gaps: Weather derivatives are illiquid; corporate hedge, not a trading rule
rule_summary: Build temperature indexes from daily average temperature Ti = (Tmin+Tmax)/2 with Tbase = 65°F: CDD = sum of max(0, Ti − Tbase) and HDD = sum of max(0, Tbase − Ti) over the contract life (week, month or season). Hedge the weather-sensitive part of demand q_w with weather derivatives. For HDD risk, short HDD futures or buy HDD puts. For CDD risk, go long CDD futures or buy CDD calls. Hedge ratios equal Cov(q_w, payoff)/Var(payoff), with the sign as given in the formulas (the put ratio has a minus sign).
backtest_note: This is a hedge for a company's own demand, not a standalone trading rule. Testing it needs firm-specific demand data and weather-derivative prices, which trade thinly.
name_es: Riesgo del clima – cobertura de la demanda

name: Energy—Spark Spread
required_data: electricity futures prices; natural gas futures prices; power plant heat rate; contract sizes
data_sources: GAP: power and natural gas futures history (CME/ICE)
gaps: Power futures are not in our data
rule_summary: Sell electricity futures and buy natural gas futures to form a spark spread S = PE − H·PF, where H is the plant's heat rate (MMBtu/Mwh). The hedge ratio is h = H·FE/FF, with FE = 736 Mwh and FF = 10,000 MMBtu. Approximate h as a ratio of integers NF/NE with the smallest possible denominator, then buy NF gas contracts for every NE electricity contracts sold. Producers use the position as a hedge, and speculators use it as a bet on a power plant's margin.
backtest_note: The text gives no entry, exit or timing rules, so the heat rate and holding period must be assumed. Electricity futures data also differ by region.

name: Buying and Holding Distressed Debt
required_data: corporate bond prices and yields; Treasury yields by tenor; default and bankruptcy filing dates; bond seniority and industry classification
data_sources: GAP: distressed bond prices
gaps: Bond-level data
rule_summary: Buy the debt of distressed companies at a deep discount and hold it, expecting the company to repay or reorganize successfully. A bond counts as distressed when its yield spread over Treasuries is above a set threshold, for example 1,000 bps. Spread the portfolio across industries, issuers, and debt seniority and quality. Positions are often opened on key dates, such as the end of the month of a default or bankruptcy filing, to profit from market overreaction.
backtest_note: Distressed bonds trade over the counter, so prices are thin and hard to get, and recovery and exit choices need modelling assumptions.
name_es: Inversión pasiva en deuda en distress

name: Active Distressed Investing
required_data: distressed security prices; bankruptcy/restructuring filings; capital structure data
gaps: Active control of a bankrupt company; not a market rule
rule_summary: Buy the debt or other securities of a distressed company to gain some control over how it is managed and reorganized. This differs from the passive approach. The company may reorganize under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection or work directly with its creditors out of court. The investor uses its stake to influence the reorganization outcome.
backtest_note: Returns depend on gaining control and on negotiated reorganization outcomes, not on a systematic rule, so a backtest is not possible.
name_es: Inversión activa en activos en distress

name: Planning a Reorganization
required_data: bankruptcy filings; distressed debt holdings and prices; court reorganization proceedings
gaps: Active control of a bankrupt company; not a market rule
rule_summary: The investor buys a substantial stake in a bankrupt company's debt and files a reorganization plan with the bankruptcy court. The aim is to gain some role in running the company, raise its value, and profit. Plans filed by large debt holders tend to be more competitive.
backtest_note: The strategy depends on active legal involvement and court outcomes, not on a mechanical trading rule.

name: Buying Outstanding Debt
required_data: distressed debt prices; bankruptcy/reorganization filings; restructuring terms
gaps: Active control of a bankrupt company; not a market rule
rule_summary: Buy the outstanding debt of a distressed company at a large discount. The bet is that after the reorganization, part of this debt turns into equity, which gives the investor some control over the company.
backtest_note: This is a discretionary, case-by-case control play built on illiquid OTC debt and negotiated restructuring outcomes, with no explicit systematic rule.

name: Loan-to-own
required_data: company financial condition and credit data; private loan terms; bankruptcy/reorganization outcomes
gaps: Active control of a bankrupt company; not a market rule
