rule_summary: Lend money through secured loans to a distressed company that is not yet bankrupt. The investor profits if the company recovers, avoids bankruptcy and its equity value rises. If the company files for Chapter 11 instead, the secured loan is converted into equity with control rights during the reorganization.
backtest_note: The strategy depends on privately negotiated secured loans and taking control in a restructuring, so it has no mechanical rule or public price series to test.

name: Distress Risk Puzzle
required_data: monthly stock returns; accounting/balance sheet data; market capitalization; bankruptcy/delisting events for model estimation
data_sources: FinancialDatasets (fundamentals for a failure-probability model); IBKR history (daily bars)
gaps: Failure-probability model inputs must be point-in-time
rule_summary: For each stock, estimate the probability of bankruptcy P_i, for example with a logistic regression. Short the stocks in the top decile of P_i (the riskiest) and buy the stocks in the bottom decile (the safest), which gives a zero-cost portfolio. Rebalance monthly; annual rebalancing is also possible and gives similar returns.
backtest_note: You must choose and estimate the bankruptcy-probability model (logistic regression), and that requires historical bankruptcy data and fundamentals.

name: Distress Risk Puzzle—Risk Management
required_data: daily close prices; accounting data for distress/bankruptcy probability estimation; market capitalization
data_sources: FinancialDatasets (fundamentals for a failure-probability model); IBKR history (daily bars)
gaps: Failure-probability model inputs must be point-in-time
rule_summary: Build the standard healthy-minus-distressed (HMD) zero-cost portfolio: go long financially healthy stocks and short distressed stocks, ranked by estimated bankruptcy/distress probability. Scale the position by sigma_target / sigma_hat. sigma_target is the target volatility, usually 10%-15%. sigma_hat is the strategy's realized volatility, estimated from daily returns over the past year. If you do not want leverage, cap the scale factor at min(sigma_target/sigma_hat, 1).
backtest_note: You must choose a distress-probability model (e.g. failure probability or O-score), and this section does not give the rebalance frequency.
name_es: Rompecabezas de riesgo de dificultades – gestión

name: Mixed-Asset Diversification with Real Estate
instruments: real estate / REITs; stocks; government bonds; corporate bonds
required_data: real estate return series (REIT or property index); stock and bond returns; covariance/expected return estimates
data_sources: IBKR history (REIT ETF proxies, e.g. VNQ)
gaps: REIT ETFs are a proxy for direct real estate
rule_summary: Buy and hold real estate assets as part of a traditional portfolio of stocks and bonds to get diversification, because real estate has low correlation with other assets. Set the weights with mean-variance optimization or a vector autoregressive (VAR) model, based on the investor's risk/return preferences and time horizon.
backtest_note: You can backtest this with REIT indexes, but you must choose the weights yourself (the optimizer, the horizon, and the investor's preferences), and direct property returns are appraisal-based.
name_es: Diversificación de activos mixtos con bienes raíces

name: Intra-asset Diversification Within Real Estate
required_data: property-level or regional real estate return indices; property characteristics (location, type, size); return covariances
data_sources: GAP: property-type and regional real-estate return indexes (e.g. NCREIF); FRED (house price indexes, CPI)
gaps: Index returns are appraisal-based and not tradable
rule_summary: Spread real estate holdings across several properties that differ by geographic area, property type, size, distance to a metropolitan area, and economic region. Allocation weights come from standard portfolio construction methods such as mean-variance optimization, as in Section 16.2.
backtest_note: Physical properties are illiquid and have appraisal-based returns, so a backtest needs REIT or regional index proxies and a chosen allocation method.

name: Property Type Diversification
required_data: property returns by property type (e.g., appraisal-based indices or sector REIT returns); transaction costs
data_sources: GAP: property-type and regional real-estate return indexes (e.g. NCREIF); FRED (house price indexes, CPI)
gaps: Index returns are appraisal-based and not tradable
rule_summary: Hold a real estate portfolio spread across property types such as apartments, offices, industrial properties (including manufacturing buildings), and retail shopping centers. The aim is to lower non-systematic risk. The text gives no weighting or rebalancing rules.
backtest_note: Physical property is illiquid and the rule gives no weights, so a backtest needs proxies such as sector REITs or property-type indices plus an assumed allocation scheme.
name_es: Diversificación por el tipo de propiedad

name: Economic Diversification
required_data: regional property returns; regional economic indicators (employment, income, industry mix)
data_sources: GAP: property-type and regional real-estate return indexes (e.g. NCREIF); FRED (house price indexes, CPI)
gaps: Index returns are appraisal-based and not tradable
rule_summary: Spread real estate investments across regions that are grouped by economic traits, such as main economic activity, employment statistics and average income. The goal is to cut non-systematic risk and transaction costs. The text gives no weighting or rebalancing rule.
backtest_note: Direct property data is illiquid and appraisal-based, and the text gives no rule for defining regions or setting weights, so a test has to rely on proxies such as regional REIT indices.

name: Property Type and Geographic Diversification
required_data: property-level returns or values by type and region; property type and location classification
data_sources: GAP: property-type and regional real-estate return indexes (e.g. NCREIF); FRED (house price indexes, CPI)
gaps: Index returns are appraisal-based and not tradable
rule_summary: Build a real estate portfolio diversified across two attributes at once, property type and geographic region. For example, with four property types (office, retail, industrial, residential) and four US regions (East, Midwest, South, West), spread holdings across the 16 resulting groups.
backtest_note: This applies to physical property portfolios and gives no weighting rule, so a backtest would need appraisal-based indices or REITs as proxies plus a chosen weighting scheme (e.g. equal weight).
name_es: Diversificación por el tipo de propiedad y la región

name: Real Estate Momentum—Regional Approach
required_data: regional (MSA) house price index returns; REIT prices by region; house price index futures/options prices
data_sources: GAP: property-type and regional real-estate return indexes (e.g. NCREIF); FRED (house price indexes, CPI)
gaps: Index returns are appraisal-based and not tradable
rule_summary: Buy real estate in the US metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) with the highest past returns, because past winners tend to keep outperforming and past losers tend to keep underperforming. You can build a zero-cost version by going long high-momentum regions and short low-momentum regions through REITs, or through futures and options on regional US house price indexes. The text gives no lookback period and no rebalance schedule.
backtest_note: You cannot trade physical property directly, so you must use regional REITs or thinly traded house price index derivatives as proxies, and you have to choose the lookback and rebalance periods yourself.

name: Inflation Hedging with Real Estate
required_data: real estate returns by property type; inflation rate (CPI)
data_sources: GAP: property-type and regional real-estate return indexes (e.g. NCREIF); FRED (house price indexes, CPI)
gaps: Index returns are appraisal-based and not tradable
rule_summary: Hold real estate as a hedge against inflation, because studies find real estate returns track the inflation rate. Commercial real estate may hedge better than other property types, since its prices adjust faster to inflation. The text gives no explicit entry, exit or rebalance rules.
backtest_note: The section only says real estate tends to rise with inflation and gives no trading rule, so testing it means using REITs or appraisal-based indices in place of physical property.
name_es: Cobertura contra la inflación con bienes raíces

name: Fix-and-flip
required_data: property transaction prices; renovation cost estimates; local market comparable prices
gaps: Not a tradable market strategy
rule_summary: Buy a run-down property that needs renovation at a substantial discount to market price. Renovate it, then resell it at a price high enough to cover the renovation costs and leave a profit.
backtest_note: The strategy trades individual physical properties and depends on deal-specific renovation work, so it cannot be backtested systematically.

name: Money Laundering—The Dark Side of Cash
gaps: Describes money laundering, which is illegal. Excluded.
rule_summary: This is not a trading rule. The section describes money laundering in three steps: placement (illegal cash is split into small deposits across many bank accounts), layering (the money is moved between accounts and countries to hide where it came from), and integration (the money comes back through cash-heavy businesses such as bars, restaurants, car washes and casinos). There are no positions, signals or exit rules.
backtest_note: This is an illegal activity, only described, with no market rule to test.
name_es: Lavado de dinero – el lado oscuro del efectivo

name: Liquidity Management
required_data: portfolio holdings; liquidity demand / cash flow forecasts; transaction cost estimates
gaps: Not a tradable market strategy
rule_summary: Keep the best amount of cash in the portfolio to cover liquidity needs from unexpected events, so other assets do not have to be sold at high transaction cost. Companies can also hold cash as a precaution against cash-flow shortfalls. The text gives no explicit rule for choosing the cash level.
backtest_note: This is a general idea about how much cash to hold, with no explicit trading rule or parameters to test.

name: Repurchase Agreement (REPO)
required_data: repo rates by tenor; collateral prices and haircuts
gaps: Not a tradable market strategy
rule_summary: Borrow cash at a fixed interest rate for a set term (repo) by posting assets as collateral and agreeing to buy them back from the counterparty, or lend cash against collateral and agree to sell it back (reverse repo). Terms usually run from 1 day to 6 months.
backtest_note: The text only describes a cash-equivalent funding transaction and gives no selection or timing rule to test.

name: Pawnbroking
required_data: collateral appraisal values; loan terms and interest rates; default/repayment records
gaps: Not a tradable market strategy
rule_summary: The lender gives a cash loan that carries interest and has a pre-agreed term, which can sometimes be extended. The loan is secured by valuable items such as jewelry, electronics, vehicles, rare books or musical instruments. The loan amount is usually well below the appraised value of the collateral. If the borrower does not repay on the agreed terms, the lender keeps or sells the collateral.
backtest_note: This is private secured lending against physical goods, so there is no market price data for a backtest.

name: Loan Sharking
gaps: Loan sharking is illegal in many places. Excluded.
rule_summary: The lender makes loans at very high interest rates, often with no collateral, and sometimes uses blackmail or violence to make borrowers repay. There is no trading rule for selecting securities, entering, or exiting.
backtest_note: This is an illegal private lending activity, not a market trading rule, so there is no price data to backtest.

name: Artificial Neural Network (ANN)
required_data: intraday BTC prices (e.g. 15-minute bars)
data_sources: Crypto exchange public OHLCV (Nautilus has exchange adapters)
gaps: Model training needs a walk-forward split to avoid look-ahead
rule_summary: Train an artificial neural network to forecast short-term Bitcoin moves, e.g. on 15-minute bars. Inputs are technical indicators built from mean-adjusted, volatility-normalized returns: the normalized return itself, EMAs and EMSDs with lengths of 30 min, 1 h, 3 h and 6 h, and RSIs with lengths of 3 h, 6 h and 12 h. The output layer predicts which of K quantiles the next normalized return will fall into, and you trade BTC long or short in the direction of the predicted quantile.
backtest_note: You must choose the network design, the training window, the number of quantiles and the signal-to-trade mapping yourself, and the many free parameters make overfitting likely.

name: Sentiment Analysis—Naïve Bayes Bernoulli
required_data: news/tweets text; BTC price history; keyword vocabulary
data_sources: GAP: historical tweet text for BTC keywords; Crypto exchange public OHLCV
gaps: No tweet archive
rule_summary: Collect tweets that contain keywords from a BTC-related vocabulary over a time period, clean them (remove duplicates and stop words, apply stemming), and encode each tweet as a binary (Bernoulli) feature vector showing which vocabulary words appear in it. A naïve Bayes classifier trained on past data estimates the conditional probability of each class, for example BTC going up or down, or quantiles of normalized returns. The trade goes in the direction of the most likely class: buy when up is predicted and sell when down is predicted.
backtest_note: A backtest needs historical Twitter data plus your own choices for the vocabulary, the text cleaning, the prediction horizon and the class definitions, and the text does not specify any of these.
name_es: Análisis de sentimiento – naïve Bayes Bernoulli

name: Fundamental Macro Momentum
instruments: equity index futures; FX spot; government bonds
required_data: real GDP growth by country; expected CPI / inflation forecasts; FX spot rates and export weights; short-term interest rates; equity index returns and risk-free rates; asset class prices
data_sources: FRED / OECD macro series (with release dates); IBKR history (country index, bond and FX futures/ETFs)
gaps: Macro data must be vintage (as first released)
rule_summary: For each country, compute 1-year trends in four macro state variables: business cycle (1-year change in real GDP growth and expected CPI, 50% weight each), international trade (1-year change in FX spot vs an export-weighted basket), monetary policy (1-year change in short-term rates), and risk sentiment (1-year equity market excess return). Rank assets within each class (e.g., country equity indexes, currencies, government bonds) by these scores, using the sign that matches how each trend affects that asset class. Go long the top decile and short the bottom decile. Combine the asset-class portfolios with equal weights and hold each position for 3 to 6 months.
backtest_note: The text does not say how to combine the four variables or set the sign for each asset class, and the expected-CPI and macro data must be point-in-time.

name: Global Macro Inflation Hedge
required_data: headline CPI year-over-year; core CPI year-over-year; commodity futures/ETF prices
data_sources: FRED / OECD macro series (with release dates); IBKR history (country index, bond and FX futures/ETFs)
gaps: Macro data must be vintage (as first released)
rule_summary: Set the commodity share of the portfolio to CA = max(0, min((HI_YoY − CI_YoY)/HI_YoY, 1)), where HI is year-over-year headline inflation and CI is year-over-year core inflation. Take the commodity exposure by buying a basket of commodities through ETFs or futures. Recompute the share whenever new inflation data is released.
backtest_note: The text does not specify the commodity basket, what the rest of the portfolio holds, or how to handle inflation data release lags.
name_es: Cobertura macro global contra la inflación

name: Global Fixed-Income Strategy
required_data: country bond ETF prices; GDP by country; inflation by country; sovereign risk measures (e.g. CDS spreads or ratings); real interest rates; output gap estimates; government yield curves by tenor; forward rates for Cochrane-Piazzesi factor
data_sources: FRED / OECD macro series (with release dates); IBKR history (country index, bond and FX futures/ETFs)
gaps: Macro data must be vintage (as first released)
rule_summary: Rank government bonds (usually country bond ETFs) of different countries cross-sectionally on macro and market factors: GDP, inflation, sovereign risk, real interest rates, output gap, value, momentum, yield-curve term spread, and the Cochrane-Piazzesi predictor. Buy the bonds in the top quantile and sell those in the bottom quantile to form a zero-cost portfolio. You can also combine several factors into a multifactor ranking.
backtest_note: The text does not specify how to define the factors, how to combine them, the quantile cutoffs, or the rebalance frequency, so the monthly frequency is an assumption; cross-country macro data must also be aligned with release dates.

name: Trading on Economic Announcements
instruments: ETFs; equity index futures; government bonds; cash / money market
required_data: daily close prices; FOMC and other macro announcement calendar; risk-free rate
data_sources: FOMC and macro release calendar (public); IBKR history (SPY, T-bill ETF)
rule_summary: Hold 100% in equities (through an index ETF or equity index futures) on days with major economic announcements, such as FOMC announcements. On all other days, hold 100% in risk-free assets (Treasury bills or bonds). You can add filters, for example technical filters.
backtest_note: The text does not define which announcements count as major, and it does not say exactly when to enter and exit around each announcement day.
